title: First falsehoods of the Ubiquitarians: without infinite flesh the hypostatic union supposedly dissolves
pass_a_gloss: The first falsehoods of those theologians who are commonly called Ubiquitarians, and of whom the harsher — and also the chiefs — were the Swabians, were many. For example: that the hypostatic union of the natures is dissolved if the human is not made commensurate with the divine, equally infinite, omnipresent, and so on. The retorsion is ready to hand: that that personal union is destroyed by the portent of ubiquity. Thus they supposed that "the whole Christ," said of the person and of the subject-which (subjectum quod), and "the whole of Christ," said of the united natures or the subject-by-which (subjectum quo), are one and the same.
pass_b_english: Those theologians commonly called Ubiquitarians had many first falsehoods. The harsher among them — and their chiefs — were the Swabians.
One sample: they say the hypostatic union of the natures dissolves unless the human nature is stretched to match the divine — equally infinite, equally omnipresent, and so on.
Turn the charge around and it is ready: the marvel of ubiquity is what cancels that personal union.

On that path they collapsed two phrases into one: "the whole Christ," said of the person and of the subject-which (subjectum quod), and "the whole of Christ," said of the united natures or the subject-by-which (subjectum quo).
source_text: Πρῶτα ψεύδη eorum Theologorum qui vulgo Ubiquitarii, & quorum duriores sed & principes Suevi, fuere plurima. Ex. gr. solvi Unionem Hypostaticam Naturarum, si Humana Divinae non sit commensurata, aeque infinita, omnipraesens, &c. Retorsione in promptu; tolli eam Personalem Unionem portento Ubiquitatis: Sic supposuere, Totum Christum, quod dictum de Persona, & subjecto quod, ac Totum Christi, quod de Naturis unitis, vel subjecto quo, unum & idem esse.
